concepts.title: Indus Valley cities
concepts.hook: At Mohenjo-daro, streets meet at right angles and covered drains run along them. No one can read the city's writing yet. So how do we know it was planned?
concepts.rule: Mohenjo-daro's lower town has streets that cross at right angles, and every street had a drain. The Indus script is still unread, so we learn about the city from its ruins.

claims.text: In Mohenjo-daro's lower town, buildings line streets that cross at right angles. This shows an early kind of town planning.
All the streets and lanes of Mohenjo-daro had drains. Most were covered with baked bricks, and pipes and chutes from houses led into them.
The Indus script is still not deciphered, so experts learn about the cities from what survives.
The Great Bath pool is some 39 feet, about 12 metres, long, with a flight of steps at each end.
The ruins cover about 240 hectares, and only about a third has been dug since digging began in 1922.

items.stem: On a school trip to a new Delhi colony, Arjun sees roads meeting at square corners in neat blocks. What does that tell him?

options.text: Planners laid it out first.
options.feedback: Like Mohenjo-daro's lower town, a neat grid shows someone drew the plan before building.

options.text: The roads grew out of old cattle paths over time.
options.feedback: Cattle paths wind and bend. Square corners in neat blocks point to a plan.

options.text: Every house was built by one family.
options.feedback: Who built the houses is not shown by the grid. The grid shows a plan.

items.stem: Diggers find streets that meet at right angles. From this pattern they work back to a ___ behind the town.

options.text: Plan.
options.feedback: A neat grid does not happen by chance, so it points back to a plan.

options.text: Flood.
options.feedback: Floods wash things away. They do not lay out square street corners.

options.text: Accident of nature.
options.feedback: Nature makes curves and bends. Right angles point to people planning.

items.stem: A friend says ancient towns grew with no plan at all. Why does Mohenjo-daro's lower town not fit that?

options.text: Its streets cross at right angles in neat blocks.
options.feedback: A regular grid of streets is a sign of planning, which goes against the friend's claim.

options.text: It sat beside a river, which made planning pointless.
options.feedback: A river does not cancel planning. The street grid itself shows a plan.

options.text: Its people had no tools to build lanes.
options.feedback: They built brick houses and drains, so tools were not lacking.

items.stem: During the monsoon, a Mumbai street floods because its drain is choked with silt. Which Mohenjo-daro feature dealt with silt?

options.text: Pools in the drains that let mud sink.
options.feedback: Settling pools let mud collect, so the water could keep flowing.

options.text: Drains left open to the sky with no covers.
options.feedback: Most Mohenjo-daro drains were covered. The pools are what caught the mud.

options.text: A well beside each house.
options.feedback: Wells gave water for use. They did nothing to stop mud in the drains.

items.stem: A guide says Mohenjo-daro's drains were open ditches dug in the mud. What is not quite right?

options.text: Most were brick channels with covers.
options.feedback: The drains were built of fitted baked bricks, and most were covered and hidden.

options.text: The city had no drains of any kind.
options.feedback: Every street and lane had a drain, so the city was far from drainless.

options.text: The drains were made of iron.
options.feedback: They were built of baked brick, not metal.

items.stem: Which pair of finds best shows the city followed a shared plan?

options.text: Grid streets and a drain on every street.
options.feedback: A street grid plus drains on every street means many people worked to one plan.

options.text: One big pool and a single carved seal.
options.feedback: One pool and one seal could come from a few people. They do not show a citywide plan.

options.text: A few fine pots and some beads.
options.feedback: Pots and beads show craft skill, not a plan for the whole city.

items.stem: About 80 hectares of this Indus city have been dug, roughly a third of it. About how big is the whole site?

options.text: About 240 hectares.
options.feedback: If 80 is about a third, the whole is about three times 80, which is 240.

options.text: About 110 hectares.
options.feedback: That adds a third again. If 80 is a third, the whole is about 240.

options.text: About 27 hectares.
options.feedback: That divides by three. A third of the site is 80, so the whole is larger.

options.text: Steps at both ends of the Great Bath
options.feedback: Steps going down show that people could walk into the water.

options.text: People could walk down into the water
options.feedback: We know this from the steps, even though the pool's exact use is unclear.

options.text: Streets crossing at right angles
options.feedback: A neat grid shows the town was laid out in advance.

options.text: A layout decided in advance
options.feedback: This comes from the right-angle street grid of the lower town.

options.text: Covered brick drains
options.feedback: Brick covers kept the waste hidden from view.

options.text: Waste kept out of sight
options.feedback: This is what the covered brick drains did.

misconceptions.correction: The Great Bath is a big public pool. No writing tells us its exact use.

misconceptions.name: A seal gives us a translation
misconceptions.correction: Experts have not yet found a sure way to read the Indus signs.

misconceptions.name: Old towns grew with no plan
misconceptions.correction: Mohenjo-daro's right-angle streets show that its lower town was planned.

misconceptions.name: Old drains were open ditches
misconceptions.correction: Most Mohenjo-daro drains were channels of baked brick with covers on top.

steps.title: Streets laid out on a plan

hook.stem: Streets that cross each other at neat right angles usually point to what?

options.text: Someone planned the layout.
options.feedback: Right. Regular crossings like these rarely happen by chance, so they point to a plan.

options.text: Paths grew wherever people liked to walk.
options.feedback: Paths made by walking bend and wander. Neat right angles point to a plan instead.

options.text: The whole city was built in a day.
options.feedback: A plan does not mean speed. The grid shows design, not how fast it was built.

steps.teach: In Mohenjo-daro's lower town, streets cross at right angles in neat blocks. A grid like this does not grow by chance, so it shows the town was planned.

example.ask: Tap the sign of planning.
parts: Diggers uncovered the lower town,
where streets meet at right angles,
and brick houses line each street.
example.spot: where streets meet at right angles,
example.feedback: Right-angle crossings show the streets were laid out on a plan.

guided.stem: A map shows straight streets meeting at square corners. What is the best reading?
guided.hint: Ask how such a neat pattern could come about.

options.text: The town was planned.
options.feedback: Yes. A regular grid is a sign that people planned the streets.

options.text: Rivers carved the streets.
options.feedback: Rivers make curves, not square corners. The grid points to planning.

options.text: Each family made its own path to the river.
options.feedback: Separate choices would not line up so neatly. A shared plan would.

guided.stem: In which part of Mohenjo-daro do the right-angle streets lie?
guided.hint: Look away from the high mound in the west.

options.text: The lower town.
options.feedback: Right. The grid of streets lies in the lower town, east of the high mound.

options.text: The high mound in the west.
options.feedback: The high western mound is a separate area. The street grid is in the lower town.

options.text: A village far outside the city.
options.feedback: The grid is inside the city, in its lower town.

steps.takeaway: Right-angle streets show Mohenjo-daro was planned.

steps.title: Drains ran along every street

hook.stem: Where do you think used water from Mohenjo-daro's homes went?

options.text: Into drains along the street.
options.feedback: Right. Pipes and chutes led from houses into drains that ran along every street.

options.text: Straight onto the open road outside.
options.feedback: The city had drains on every street, so water did not just spill onto the road.

options.text: Into each family's well.
options.feedback: Wells gave clean water. Used water went out to the street drains.

steps.teach: Every street and lane had a drain. Pipes and chutes carried used water from homes into them. Most drains had brick covers, so the waste stayed out of sight.

nodes: Pipe or chute in the wall

example.ask: Tap where the used water ends up.
parts: A family washes on the bathing floor,
the water runs down a pipe in the wall,
and flows into the covered street drain.
example.spot: and flows into the covered street drain.
example.feedback: House pipes fed the street drains, which carried the water away.

guided.stem: What were most street drains in Mohenjo-daro made of?
guided.hint: Think of what the city's houses were built from.

options.text: Baked bricks.
options.feedback: Yes. The drains were built of closely fitted baked bricks.

options.text: Wooden planks nailed together.
options.feedback: Wood was not the drain material. The channels were baked brick.

options.text: Metal pipes.
options.feedback: The street drains were brick channels, not metal pipes.

guided.stem: Small pools were built into the drains. What did they catch?
guided.hint: Heavy bits sink when water slows down.

options.text: Mud and waste that settled out.
options.feedback: Right. Settling pools let mud collect while the water flowed on.

options.text: Rain kept for drinking later.
options.feedback: These pools sat inside the waste drains, so they held sludge, not drinking water.

options.text: Fish for food.
options.feedback: The pools were part of the drain system. They trapped mud and waste.

steps.takeaway: House pipes fed covered brick drains along every street.

steps.title: The script is unread, so ruins tell the story

hook.stem: Indus seals carry short rows of signs. Can experts read them today?

options.text: Not yet; the script is unread.
options.feedback: Right. The Indus script has not been deciphered, so the signs stay a puzzle.

options.text: Yes, each seal has been translated.
options.feedback: No seal has a sure reading yet. The script is still not deciphered.

options.text: Yes, they name each king.
options.feedback: We cannot name rulers from the signs, because no one can read them yet.

steps.teach: No one can read the Indus script yet, and just a third of the city has been dug. So we learn from what survives: streets, drains, baths and seals.

example.ask: Tap the limit on what we know.
parts: The Great Bath is about 12 metres long,
but no writing we can read explains it,
so experts still argue about its use.
example.spot: but no writing we can read explains it,
example.feedback: We can measure the pool, but without readable writing its exact use stays open.

guided.stem: A poster says an Indus seal is a king's signed order. What is the problem?
guided.hint: Ask whether anyone can make sense of the marks.

options.text: No one can read the signs yet.
options.feedback: Right. With the script unread, no seal can be called a king's order.

options.text: Seals were children's toys.
options.feedback: We do not know that either. The real problem is that the signs are unread.

options.text: Kings in that age used no seals.
options.feedback: That is a guess too. The point is that no one can read these signs.

guided.stem: The Great Bath has steps at each end. What can we say for sure?
guided.hint: Keep what you can see apart from what you guess.

options.text: People could walk down into the pool.
options.feedback: Yes. Steps at each end show people could go in and out.

options.feedback: Nothing we can read says who used it. That is a guess.

options.text: It was a royal palace.
options.feedback: It is a large pool with rooms around it. No text calls it a palace.

steps.takeaway: Indus signs are unread, so ruins carry the story.

concepts.title: Ashoka's edicts
concepts.hook: Ashoka had messages carved on rocks and polished pillars across his empire. One pillar still stands about 32 feet high. Why carve words into stone?
concepts.rule: Ashoka carved messages on rocks, then on pillars, across his empire. The language and script changed by region. His message, dhamma, asked for respect and kindness.

claims.text: Ashoka had edicts carved on rocks and later on pillars across his empire.
A stone pillar at Lauriya Nandagarh in Bihar still stands. It is about 32 feet tall, with a seated lion on top.
Most of Ashoka's edicts were in Prakrit, mostly in the Brahmi script. Some in the northwest used Kharosthi. Those in Afghanistan used Greek and Aramaic.
Ashoka's dhamma asked people to respect elders and be kind to servants. It also asked them to respect other faiths.
Most people then could probably not read, so special officers were sent to spread the message of dhamma.

items.stem: A Delhi school club wants a notice to survive outdoors for centuries. Which choice copies Ashoka's method?

options.text: Carve it into stone.
options.feedback: Ashoka's carved rocks and pillars have lasted over two thousand years outdoors.

options.text: Print it on glossy paper posters.
options.feedback: Paper tears and fades in sun and rain within months, not centuries.

options.text: Paint it on cloth banners.
options.feedback: Cloth rots outdoors quickly. Carved stone is what lasted for Ashoka.

items.stem: Ashoka's pillar at Lauriya Nandagarh is close to 10 metres tall. With a foot at about 0.3 metres, about how many feet is that?

options.text: About 33 feet.
options.feedback: Ten divided by 0.3 is about 33, which fits the pillar's height of about 32 feet.

options.text: About 3 feet.
options.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing. Ten metres is far taller than a child.

options.text: About 300 feet.
options.feedback: That is far too tall. Ten divided by 0.3 is about 33.

items.stem: A quiz answer says Ashoka kept his edicts inside his palace for his court to read. What is not quite right?

options.text: They were carved in public places across the empire.
options.feedback: Rock edicts stood near towns and routes, and pillars rose across the empire.

options.text: He wrote them on paper scrolls.
options.feedback: They were carved in stone, on rocks and pillars, not on paper.

options.text: He had no court.
options.feedback: He did have a court. The point is that the edicts stood in public places.

items.stem: Which language did most of Ashoka's edicts use?

options.text: Prakrit.
options.feedback: Most Ashokan edicts were in Prakrit, a language people spoke at the time.

options.text: Sanskrit, the language of later court poems.
options.feedback: Early scholars guessed Sanskrit, but the earliest inscriptions were in fact in Prakrit.

options.text: Greek.
options.feedback: Just a few edicts in Afghanistan use Greek. Most are in Prakrit.

items.stem: In a college museum, two Ashokan inscriptions sit side by side: one in Brahmi, one in Greek. What best explains the difference?

options.text: They come from different regions.
options.feedback: Brahmi was used in most of the empire, while Greek was used in Afghanistan.

options.text: One of them must be a modern fake made to fool visitors.
options.feedback: Both scripts were really used. Greek edicts are known from Afghanistan.

options.text: Ashoka changed scripts each year.
options.feedback: The change follows place, not time. Region decided the script.

items.stem: A train station notice in Chennai uses Tamil, Hindi and English. Like Ashoka's edicts, its script changes with the ___.

options.text: Region.
options.feedback: The script fits the place, as Ashoka's edicts did from Bengal to Afghanistan.

options.text: Season.
options.feedback: Notices do not change with the weather. They change with the place.

options.text: Mood of whoever painted it.
options.feedback: The choice is not random. It follows the region the notice is in.

items.stem: A website says Ashoka's edicts just told people to obey the king. What does it miss?

options.text: They asked for respect and kindness too.
options.feedback: Dhamma asked people to respect elders, treat servants kindly and respect other faiths.

options.text: They were about trade taxes and market prices.
options.feedback: The dhamma edicts were about how to treat others, not about taxes.

options.text: They held no messages, just names.
options.feedback: The edicts carry long messages about conduct, not just names.

options.text: Greeting a grandparent with care
options.feedback: This everyday act shows the respect for elders that dhamma asked for.

options.text: Kindness to servants

options.text: Speaking gently to a helper

options.text: Respect for other faiths

steps.title: Messages carved on rocks, then pillars

hook.stem: A ruler wants his words to reach far-off towns and last for centuries. What would work best?

options.text: Carve them on stone near busy routes.
options.feedback: Right. Ashoka carved messages on rocks near towns and routes, and many still survive.

options.text: Write them on palm leaves kept safe at court.
options.feedback: Leaves at court reach few people and rot in time. Stone in public lasts.

options.text: Have a herald shout them in the capital.
options.feedback: A shout fades at once and reaches one city. Carved stone lasts and travels further.

steps.teach: Ashoka carved messages on rocks near towns and routes, so passers-by could see them. Years later, he added polished pillars. Stone lasts, so some still stand.

guided.stem: Which came first in Ashoka's carving plan?

options.text: Edicts on rocks.
options.feedback: Yes. The rock edicts came first; pillar edicts were added years later.

options.text: Edicts on tall polished pillars.

steps.title: Written in the region's own script

hook.stem: Ashoka ruled from the far northwest to Bengal. Would one script fit every edict?

options.text: No, the script changed with the region.
options.feedback: Right. Most edicts use Brahmi, but some in the northwest use Kharosthi, Greek or Aramaic.

options.text: Yes, every edict used the Brahmi script.
options.feedback: Most did, but not all. Edicts in the northwest and Afghanistan used other scripts.

options.text: Yes, each one was in Greek.
options.feedback: Greek was used just in Afghanistan. Most edicts are in Prakrit, written in Brahmi.

steps.teach: Most edicts use Prakrit in the Brahmi script. Some in the northwest use Kharosthi, and those in Afghanistan use Greek. So the script changed with the region.

example.ask: Tap the script used in most edicts.
parts: His carvers wrote most edicts in Prakrit,
using the Brahmi script,
while some in Afghanistan used Greek.
example.spot: using the Brahmi script,

options.text: Greek or Aramaic.
options.feedback: Yes. The edicts in Afghanistan were written in Greek and Aramaic.

options.text: Brahmi, the same as near Patna.
options.feedback: Brahmi was used in most of the empire, but Afghanistan's edicts used Greek and Aramaic.

options.text: Devanagari.

guided.stem: Most scripts for modern Indian languages grew out of which old script?
guided.hint: Think of the script in most of the edicts.

options.text: Brahmi.
options.feedback: Right. Most scripts used for modern Indian languages come from Brahmi.

options.text: Greek, from the far northwest.
options.feedback: Greek was used for a few edicts in Afghanistan. Modern Indian scripts come from Brahmi.

options.text: Aramaic.
options.feedback: Aramaic appears in the far northwest. Brahmi is the parent of most Indian scripts.

steps.takeaway: Ashoka's edicts changed language and script from region to region.

steps.title: What dhamma asked people to do

hook.stem: Ashoka's word dhamma shows up in many edicts. What did it mostly ask for?

options.text: Respect and kindness in daily life.
options.feedback: Right. Dhamma asked people to respect elders, treat servants kindly and respect other faiths.

options.text: Higher taxes to pay for a bigger army.
options.feedback: The dhamma edicts were about how to live, not about taxes.

options.text: New rules for trade in markets.
options.feedback: Dhamma was about conduct toward others, not market rules.

steps.teach: Dhamma meant a good way to live. It asked people to respect elders, be kind to servants and respect other faiths. Few could read, so officers spread it.

example.ask: Tap the part about other faiths.
parts: The edict asks people to honour their elders,
to treat their servants kindly,
and to respect religions not their own.
example.spot: and to respect religions not their own.
example.feedback: Respect for other people's religions was part of Ashoka's dhamma.

guided.stem: Most people then could not read. How did dhamma reach them?
guided.hint: Think of who travelled out to tell people.

options.text: Officers spread the message.
options.feedback: Right. Special officers were sent out to spread the message of dhamma.

options.text: Every home was handed a written copy.
options.feedback: Few people could read, and copies were not handed out. Officers carried the message.

options.text: Schools taught each edict.
options.feedback: Nothing says schools taught the edicts. Special officers spread the message.

guided.hint: Think of how you treat someone with grey hair.

options.feedback: Yes. Respect for elders was a key part of dhamma.

concepts.title: Silk Road ideas
concepts.hook: A Buddhist centre stood at a desert oasis where traders rested. Who paid for it, and how did its art style get so far from Gandhara?
concepts.rule: The Silk Road was a web of sea, river and land routes. Trade wealth paid for Buddhist art in Gandhara. Monks and traders carried ideas and art styles to new places.

claims.text: Goods went up the Indus River to Gandhara. From there they went on to China, through Afghanistan or over high passes and across Central Asia.
By about 50 BCE, ships used monsoon winds to cross the Arabian Sea to ports on India's west coast.
By the fifth century, Buddhism had thrived in Gandhara and the Swat Valley for about 600 years, paid for by trade through the Khyber and Karakorum passes.
Monks from Gandhara moved into Afghanistan and Central Asia. Their art style then grew popular at Buddhist sites there.
In Central Asia, Buddhist centres grew at oases and towns that were rest stops for traders crossing the deserts.

items.stem: A bale of Chinese silk heads for a port on India's west coast. Put its trip in order.

options.text: Leaves China for Central Asia.
options.feedback: The trip starts in China, heading west into Central Asia.

options.text: Crosses high passes down to Gandhara.
options.feedback: From Central Asia, goods came over the high passes into Gandhara.

options.text: Goes down the Indus River.
options.feedback: From Gandhara, the Indus River leads south toward the sea.

options.text: Reaches a west coast port.
options.feedback: The river trip ends at a port on India's west coast.

items.stem: For a school project, a team plans to sail cloth from Gujarat to the Red Sea. What will they wait for?

options.text: The right season's winds.
options.feedback: Sailors timed trips to the monsoon winds, which crossed the Arabian Sea.

options.text: A full moon so the sea turns calm and smooth.
options.feedback: A calm sea gives no push. The seasonal winds moved the ships.

options.text: A new road to be built.
options.feedback: This trip is by sea. The ships needed the seasonal winds.

items.stem: The Silk Road was not one road but a ___ of linked routes.

options.text: Network.
options.feedback: Many sea, river and land routes linked up, forming a network.

options.text: Single lane.
options.feedback: A single lane would be one road. The Silk Road was many linked routes.

options.text: Circle.
options.feedback: The routes did not loop in a ring. They formed a web, or network.

items.stem: A quiet valley far from any trade route has fine stone. Why might it still have little Buddhist art?

options.text: With no trade, there was little wealth to pay for it.
options.feedback: In Gandhara, trade wealth paid for the art. A valley off the routes lacked that money.

options.text: Stone cannot be carved without sea air.
options.feedback: Stone can be carved anywhere. The missing piece was money from trade.

options.text: Buddhist art was banned in valleys.
options.feedback: No such ban is known. The valley simply lacked trade wealth.

items.stem: Along the Silk Road, Buddhism had thrived in Gandhara for 24 generations of 25 years by the fifth century. About how many years is that?

options.text: About 600 years.
options.feedback: Twenty-four times 25 is 600, so Buddhism had thrived there for six centuries.

options.text: About 50 years.
options.feedback: That adds the numbers. Multiply 24 by 25 to get about 600.

options.text: About 2,400 years.
options.feedback: That uses 100 years a generation. With 25 years, it is about 600.

items.stem: A college fest in Bengaluru is paid for by local shop sponsors. Which Gandhara pattern does that match?

options.feedback: Shops fund the fest much as trade wealth paid for Buddhist art in Gandhara.

options.text: Art paying for the trade routes and their upkeep.
options.feedback: The money flowed the other way. Trade wealth paid for the art.

options.text: Monks paying traders to travel.
options.feedback: Nothing says monks paid traders. Trade wealth paid for the art.

concepts.title: Indian place value and zero
concepts.hook: Write 205, then rub out the zero. Now it says 25. One small sign changed the value by 180. What job was the zero doing?
concepts.rule: In place value, a zero marks an empty place. Brahmagupta gave rules for using zero as a number. Indian digits later spread west through Arabic books to Europe.

claims.text: In the Indian base ten system, zero can mark an empty place in a number.
Brahmagupta gave rules for zero in the seventh century. Take a number from itself and you get zero. Times zero, any number gives zero.
A scholar wrote in Arabic about India's digits 1 to 9 and 0. His name was al-Khwarizmi. Later, Fibonacci took them to Europe.
The Babylonians used a place-value system for over 1,000 years without a zero to mark empty places.

items.stem: A shop bill in Delhi should read ₹1,050, but the clerk drops the zero after the 1. What amount shows?

options.text: ₹1,500, since the 5 moves up.
options.feedback: That moves the 5 up a place. Dropping that zero gives 150.

options.text: About 9 times.
options.feedback: That is far too small. 79 times 9 is only 711.

options.text: About 900 times, since three places moved.
options.feedback: That is far too big. 79 times 900 would be over 70,000.

items.stem: A classmate says zero is useless because it stands for nothing. What is wrong with that?

options.feedback: Zero marks empty places, so it keeps numbers like 307 and 37 apart.

options.text: Zero matters for money and nowhere else.
options.feedback: Zero matters in every number with an empty place, not just money.

options.text: Zero is used in computers.
options.feedback: That is true but misses the point. Zero marks empty places in any number.

items.stem: By Brahmagupta's rule, some number minus 9 gives zero. That number is ___.

options.feedback: A number minus itself is zero, so the number must be 9.
Eighteen minus 9 is 9, not zero. The number must equal 9.
One minus 9 goes below zero. The number must be 9 itself.

items.stem: In a maths exam, Neha writes 6 − 6 = 6. Which of Brahmagupta's rules shows her slip?

options.text: A number minus itself is zero.
options.feedback: By this rule, 6 minus 6 is zero, so her answer of 6 is wrong.

options.text: A number minus itself stays the same as it was.
options.feedback: That is not his rule. Taking a number from itself leaves zero.

options.text: You cannot take a number from itself.
options.feedback: You can. Brahmagupta said the answer is zero.

items.stem: Which line best explains the two jobs zero does?

options.text: It marks the end of a number and has no other job.

options.text: It means nothing, so it has no rules.

options.text: Al-Khwarizmi writes about the digits in Arabic.

concepts.title: Printing and reading
concepts.hook: A Korean book printed with metal type came 77 years before Gutenberg's Bible. So who really invented printing?
concepts.rule: Movable type uses separate pieces that can be reset for each page. Bi Sheng made clay type in China, Korea printed with metal type, and Gutenberg's metal type spread print in Europe.

claims.text: Bi Sheng invented movable type in China between 1041 and 1048, using type made of baked clay.
Because Chinese uses so many characters, block printing stayed the main method there.
Jikji, printed in Cheongju, Korea, in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed from movable metal type. It came 77 years before the Gutenberg Bible.
Gutenberg is credited with metal type that was uniform and could be swapped. His Bible was probably finished in Mainz in 1455.
Printing put knowledge within reach of every person who knew how to read.

concepts.hook: The East India Company came to trade in cloth and spices. In time it collected the land revenue of Bengal. How did a trading company end up ruling?
concepts.rule: The Company began in 1600 with a charter to trade. After Plassey and Buxar, the 1765 diwani gave it Bengal's revenue. In 1858 a new Act moved its powers to the British Crown.

claims.text: In 1600 the East India Company got a charter from Queen Elizabeth I. It gave the Company the sole English right to trade with the East.
A factory was a trading post where Company traders, called factors, worked and stored goods. The first English factory on the Hugli came in 1651.

concepts.title: Independence and Constitution
concepts.hook: India's Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 but came into force on 26 January 1950. Why two dates, two months apart?
concepts.rule: The Constituent Assembly first met in December 1946. Its Drafting Committee, led by Ambedkar, wrote a draft. The whole Assembly debated it. It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

claims.text: The Constituent Assembly first met in New Delhi on 9 December 1946. Most members were picked by the provincial assemblies. Others stood for the princely states.
On 29 August 1947, the Assembly set up a Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar, to prepare a draft.
While debating the draft, the Assembly took up and settled 2,473 of the 7,635 changes put forward.
The Assembly adopted the text on 26 November 1949. It then came into force on 26 January 1950.
The work took two years, eleven months and seventeen days, over eleven sessions and 165 days.
Members signed it on 24 January 1950. The start date was picked because in 1929 the Congress had asked people to mark 26 January each year.
On 26 January 1950 the Assembly became a stand-in Parliament until a new one was formed in 1952.

options.text: The Assembly adopts the Constitution.
options.feedback: Adoption came last, after the long debate on the draft.

items.stem: A school chart says the Constitution was passed and came into force on the same day. What is not quite right?

options.text: It came into force about two months after it was passed.
options.feedback: It was adopted first, then came into force about two months later, in the new year.

options.text: It was not passed by anyone.
options.feedback: It was passed by the Assembly before it came into force.

options.text: It came into force ten years before it was passed.
options.feedback: A law cannot start before it is passed. It started two months after.

steps.title: A chosen Assembly made the Constitution

hook.stem: Who do you think wrote India's Constitution?

options.text: An Assembly of members from across India.
options.feedback: Right. The Constituent Assembly, with members from the provinces and princely states, made it.

options.text: One leader, working alone at a desk for many months.
options.feedback: Many members worked on it together over almost three years.

options.text: The British Parliament.
options.feedback: It was made in New Delhi by India's own Constituent Assembly.

steps.teach: The body that wrote the Constitution first met in December 1946. Most members were picked by the provinces, the rest came from princely states, so many regions had a voice.

example.ask: Tap where the Assembly first met.
parts: On a winter morning, members met
in the Constitution Hall in New Delhi,
for the very first sitting.
example.spot: in the Constitution Hall in New Delhi,
example.feedback: The first sitting was in the Constitution Hall, now the Central Hall of Parliament.

guided.stem: How were most Assembly members chosen?
guided.hint: They were not picked by voters at a booth.

options.text: By members of the provincial assemblies.
options.feedback: Yes. Most were chosen by indirect election through the provincial assemblies.

options.text: By a direct vote of every adult in the land.
options.feedback: The vote was indirect: provincial assembly members chose them.

options.text: By the British king.
options.feedback: They were chosen through the provincial assemblies, not by the king.

guided.stem: The Assembly worked for nearly three years. On how many days did it sit?
guided.hint: Think of several sessions, each a few weeks long.

options.text: 165 days.
options.feedback: Right. Its eleven sessions covered 165 days.

options.text: 16 days, about two weeks.
options.feedback: That is far too few. It sat for 165 days.

options.text: 1,000 days.
options.feedback: That is far too many. It sat for 165 days.

steps.takeaway: A large body of chosen members, not one person, wrote it.

steps.title: A draft, then debate and changes

hook.stem: A small team wrote the first draft. Was that the final text?

options.text: No, the Assembly debated and changed it.
options.feedback: Right. The full Assembly debated the draft and took up thousands of changes.

options.text: Yes, it became law with no changes made.
options.feedback: The draft was debated at length and changed before adoption.

options.text: No, London had to approve it.
options.feedback: The Assembly itself debated and adopted it in New Delhi.

steps.teach: A team led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar wrote the draft. The whole Assembly then debated it, which is why it took so long. Members put forward thousands of changes.

example.ask: Tap the Assembly's part in the work.
parts: Ambedkar's team wrote the draft,
the whole Assembly then argued over it and changed it,
and at last the final text was passed.
example.spot: the whole Assembly then argued over it and changed it,
example.feedback: The committee drafted, but the whole Assembly debated and changed the text.

guided.stem: Who chaired the Drafting Committee?
guided.hint: He was a noted jurist.

options.text: Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
options.feedback: Yes. Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

options.text: Dr Rajendra Prasad, who led many other committees.
options.feedback: Rajendra Prasad chaired other Assembly committees, not the Drafting Committee.

options.text: Jawaharlal Nehru.
options.feedback: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

guided.stem: Of 7,635 changes put forward, 2,473 were taken up. About what share is that?
guided.hint: Round both numbers first.

options.text: About a third.
options.feedback: Right. 2,473 out of 7,635 is close to one in three.

options.text: About half of them.
options.feedback: Half would be about 3,800. 2,473 is closer to a third.

options.text: Almost every one.
options.feedback: Far fewer than all were taken up, about a third.

steps.takeaway: One team wrote the draft; the whole Assembly then changed it.

steps.title: Adopted one day, in force another

hook.stem: The Constitution was adopted in November 1949. When do you think it came into force?

options.text: Two months later, in January 1950.
options.feedback: Right. It came into force on 26 January 1950.

options.text: The very same day it was adopted.
options.feedback: Adoption came first. It came into force two months later.

options.text: Ten years later.
options.feedback: The gap was about two months, not ten years.

steps.teach: The Assembly adopted the text on 26 November 1949. It came into force on 26 January 1950, because in 1929 Congress had asked people to mark that day.

example.ask: Tap the day it came into force.
parts: The Assembly adopted the text in November 1949,
members signed it on 24 January 1950,
and it came into force two days later.
example.spot: and it came into force two days later.
example.feedback: Two days after signing, on 26 January 1950, the Constitution came into force.

guided.stem: What does India celebrate each year on the day the Constitution came into force?
guided.hint: Think of the big parade on Kartavya Path.

options.text: Republic Day.
options.feedback: Right. Republic Day marks the Constitution coming into force in 1950.

options.text: Independence Day, in the middle of August.
options.feedback: Independence Day is in August. The day in January is Republic Day.

options.text: Teachers' Day.
options.feedback: That is another day. The January day is Republic Day.

guided.stem: On the day the Constitution came into force, what did the Assembly become?
guided.hint: Someone still had to make laws until a new body was chosen.

options.text: A stand-in Parliament.
options.feedback: Yes. It served as a stand-in Parliament until a new one was formed in 1952.

options.text: A high court for the whole country.
options.feedback: It did not become a court. It acted as a stand-in Parliament.

options.text: A city council.
options.feedback: It worked for the whole country, as a stand-in Parliament.

steps.takeaway: It was passed in late 1949 and came into force in 1950.
